sections.heading: 1. Do Liquids Conduct Electricity?
points: Some liquids **conduct** electricity and some do not.
**Good conductors:** solutions of **acids, bases and salts** (e.g. salt water, lemon juice) — these have **charged particles (ions)**.
A **tester** (with an LED/magnetic compass) shows whether a liquid conducts.

sections.heading: 2. Chemical Effects of Current
points: When current passes through a conducting liquid, it can cause **chemical changes** — the **chemical effect** of current.

sub: Formation of **gas bubbles** at the electrodes.

sections.heading: 3. Electroplating
points: **Electroplating** = depositing a **layer of one metal over another** using the chemical effect of electric current.

sub: **Chromium plating** on taps/car parts (shiny, resists rust).
**Tin plating** on iron cans (food storage; tin is safe/non-toxic).
**Zinc coating (galvanisation)** on iron to prevent rust.

points: The **object to be plated** is made the **cathode**; the **plating metal** the anode; the solution contains the metal's salt.

sections.heading: 4. High-Yield One-Liners (Last-Minute Recall)
points: Acid/base/salt solutions conduct (have ions); distilled water & sugar solution do not.
Chemical effect of current: gas bubbles, metal deposits, colour change at electrodes.
Electroplating = coating one metal over another using electric current.
Chromium plating (taps), tin plating (cans), silver/gold (jewellery), zinc (galvanisation).
Object to be plated = cathode; plating metal = anode.

sections.heading: 5. Common Traps (Watch Out)
points: **Distilled (pure) water is a POOR conductor**; salt/impurities make water conduct.
Conduction in liquids is due to **ions** from acids/bases/salts.
In electroplating, the **object to be plated is the cathode** (negative electrode).
**Tin plating** protects iron food cans (tin is non-toxic); **zinc coating** = galvanisation.
